bull_bear.body:
- **Debt discipline:** standalone total debt ~INR 424 cr (FY26), D/E ~0.3x, Debt/EBITDA ~1.1x; mgmt "will not like to increase debt." Cash ~INR 139 cr + ~INR 145–150 cr earmarked QIP.
- Capex funded via QIP + leasing + accruals; **working-capital squeeze (170→120–130 days)** is the stated source of growth funding for the INR 6,630 cr book. No dividend/buyback discussed.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body:
- **Changodar downtime** is the dominant risk — it single-handedly capped growth at +10% while peers did 50–60%; Q3FY27 recovery is a mgmt promise, not yet delivered.
- **CRGO DGTR anti-dumping duty** — potential RM-cost inflation; unresolved.
- **Working-capital/inventory build** — deliberate RM stocking to Dec-2026 raises interest cost near-term; unwind depends on backward-integration coming online on time.
- **Guidance-vs-reality gap** — 25% FY27 growth needs a very strong H2 after a soft H1; $1bn/FY29 implies ~50% CAGR, reframed to ~INR 8,000 cr (analysts openly pressed the math).
- **Execution stacking** — five backward-integration plants + two capacity expansions + HVDC all commissioning across FY27–28; slippage risk is high (Changodar already slipped once).
- **Management change** — new CFO Mehul Shah; IR outsourced to EY (governance-signalling after prior-year churn).
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: Confident, guidance-forward and unusually **disciplined on commitments** ("only those guidance parameters we are confident of achieving"). Candid that the +10% growth is self-inflicted (Changodar), repeatedly deflecting analyst probes on why utilization lags peers ("no major reason as such," "pretty much in line with market"). MD Mamtora crisp on HVDC/exports; CFO Mehul Shah detailed on balance sheet. EY-IR appointment + fast reporting framed as governance upgrades.
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body:
- **This is a timing air-pocket, not a demand miss** — order book +26%, inflow +218%, INR 23,000 cr pipeline; the growth simply sits behind an August-2026 Changodar restart. The Q3FY27 inflection is the whole thesis.
- **The $1bn target quietly shrank** from INR 9,600 cr to ~INR 8,000 cr (rupee reframing) — a soft downgrade dressed as an FX technicality; watch whether even INR 8,000 cr by FY29 holds given a soft FY27 base (~INR 2,500 cr FY26 → needs huge FY28–29).
- **Backward integration is now a revenue line, not just a margin lever** — INR 800–1,000 cr third-party sales feed the top-line target, so its commissioning cadence (CTC→Pressboard→Bushing→Fabrication) is doubly load-bearing.
- **Inventory build is a strategic hedge, not distress** — RM secured to Dec-2026; the interest drag is a deliberate insurance premium against geopolitical/CRGO supply shocks.
- Consol margin (19.2%) already runs well above the 16% standalone guide — subsidiaries are the quiet margin engine.

- "Capital Allocation & Funding: Capex to be funded through a balanced mix of QIP proceeds, leasing arrangements, internal accruals, and debt if required."
- "QIP Utilization: Approximately ₹145 Cr of unutilized proceeds from the 2024 QIP remains earmarked for backward integration initiatives"; the journey slide records "Successfully Raised ₹500 crores through QIP" and, earlier, "₹120 crore by way of preferential issue on private placement basis in October 2023".

bull_bear.title: Capital allocation policy (investor deck)

bull_bear.body:
- Extra-high-voltage engineering credentials: the Company built and dispatched a 333 MVA, 1200 kV auto transformer to PowerGrid's National Test Station at Bina, described as the highest AC voltage transformer in the world, and competes across the 110 kV to 1200 kV range where the number of technically qualified manufacturers falls sharply.
- Sole NABL-accredited electrical-steel testing laboratory in the Indian transformer industry, providing independent and traceable test results that serve as both a quality control and a commercial credential.
- Technology licences from Fuji Electric of Japan for 400 kV and 765 kV class reactors and generator transformers, plus a strategic alliance with ZTR Ukraine for 765 kV transformer technology, embedding continuous access to advanced global engineering practice.
- First Indian company to receive an HVDC converter transformer repair order from PowerGrid, creating a pathway to PGCIL approval of HVDC manufacturing technology that very few competitors could claim.
- Furnace-transformer franchise with among the world's largest EAF transformer ratings, including a tested 220/253 MVA electric arc furnace transformer.
- Switching costs and qualification barriers: customers cannot simply switch suppliers without restarting procurement and approval processes, and lead times of 18-24 months for 400 kV and above transformers deepen the order-book advantage of established manufacturers with proven type-testing credentials.
- Blue-chip and diversified customer base spanning PGCIL, NTPC, GETCO, UPPTCL, RRVPNL, MPPTCL and WBSECL on the utility side, Siemens, Adani, Tata Power, ReNew Power, Torrent Power and AVAADA Energy in industry and renewables, and Jindal Steel & Power, JSW, SAIL and Hindustan Zinc in metals — repeat-order relationships built order after order rather than one-off wins.
- Backward integration into CTC, bushings, pressboard and fabrication capturing margin previously paid away to third-party suppliers, evidenced by a consolidated EBITDA margin running approximately 230 basis points above standalone.
- Export footprint across 40-plus countries with relationships including ABB, ArcelorMittal, Fluor, Siemens Energy, Danieli and the Novorossiysk Group, positioned for the North American and European grid-replacement cycle.
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Raw-material price and availability risk — copper, electrical steel (CRGO) and transformer oil — Copper and CRGO dominate the cost base and copper-led inflation directly compressed FY26 margins. Management describes this as the Company's most material operational exposure because it cannot always be passed through on fixed-price contracts. Mitigation is order selection with better margins and payment terms, backward integration to internalise value, and price-variation clauses and hedging as natural further mitigants.
- Execution and capacity-ramp risk — The Changodar expansion was delayed four to five months and full backward integration has slipped slightly owing to slow site progress and late arrival of plant and machinery. Delays defer the operating leverage on which the FY28 margin recovery depends, and execution risk is the key constraint the industry itself cites for the FY26 ordering slowdown. Mitigation is a staged commissioning plan with results expected from FY28 and backward-integration facilities fully operational from Q1 FY28.
- Stretched working-capital cycle and liquidity risk — The consolidated cash conversion cycle more than doubled to 199 days from 94 days, operating cash flow turned negative, and receivables rose roughly Rs 410 crore, meaning growth is currently funded through short-term borrowing. Until the cycle normalises this constrains the ability to fund growth internally. Mitigation is intensified collections, tightened order-acceptance terms with advance collection requirements, stricter payment milestones, and a conservative net-worth-to-borrowing position.
- Single-segment and single-site geographic concentration — The Company operates in one product segment — transformer manufacturing, reported as a single segment under Ind AS 108 — with its principal manufacturing concentrated in the Ahmedabad region of Gujarat, exposing it to a single industry cycle and to location-specific operational disruption. Mitigation is the breadth of product applications across many end-markets and the multi-plant footprint within the cluster.
- Capital-expenditure funding risk — A further Rs 1000 crore of capex is planned over fifteen months, and funding this alongside a stretched working-capital cycle requires careful sequencing. Mitigation is a strengthened post-QIP equity base and modest gearing providing headroom.
- Skilled-labour availability and specialist retention — High-voltage transformer manufacturing depends on scarce specialised design, winding and testing skills — insulation design engineering, high-voltage winding and tanking, impulse and short-circuit testing, thermal modelling and dielectric diagnostics — that cannot be acquired through standard technical education. Recruiting from this small national pool commands premium compensation, and the steep rise in employee benefit expense in FY26 reflects the cost of staffing the ramp.
- Import-dependence for CRGO electrical steel — India relies substantially on imported grain-oriented electrical steel, exposing manufacturers to currency and supply risk. Mitigation is the Company's NABL steel-testing capability and supplier relationships supporting quality assurance, though supply concentration remains.
- Intensifying competition and an industry-wide ordering pause — Well-capitalised competitors are expanding aggressively — Hitachi Energy India alone reported an order backlog above Rs 29,500 crore as at March 2026, and players such as Voltamp, Atlanta Electricals and Shilchar are scaling — with competition sharpest in standard distribution and lower-voltage products. Separately, fewer utility transmission schemes were awarded in FY26 than in the prior year, and although attributed to execution rather than demand, a prolonged pause would pressure fresh order intake.
- Receivables credit risk and product-approval dependency — A large share of receivables sits with utilities and EPC customers whose payment cycles can be long, though the predominantly government-backed and blue-chip customer base lowers default risk. Sales to PGCIL and state utilities also depend on type-approvals, testing accreditation and utility procurement and tariff frameworks, mitigated by the NABL-accredited steel-testing laboratory and PGCIL approvals secured for reactors at the Changodar testing facility.

Commissioning cadence: **CRGO already live**; **CTC Q2FY27**; **Pressboard Q3FY27**; **RIP bushings Q4FY27** (the "large bottleneck" currently); **Fabrication Q1FY28**. - **Emerging demand:** data centers, railway electrification, EV-charging, renewable integration all flagged as multi-year transformer-demand layers.

outlook.body:
- Move deliberately up the voltage and complexity curve — prioritising high-margin, niche and specialty products (EHV, 1200 kV, furnace, HVDC) — as a competitive response to intense, margin-dilutive competition at the 220 kV and below level.
- Deepen backward integration to internalise CTC, pressboard, RIP bushings and fabrication, replacing input-cost volatility with a captive, quality-controlled supply chain; each facility operationalised is expected to contribute 200-300 basis points of incremental EBITDA margin.
- Establish an HVDC entry pathway by converting the PGCIL converter-transformer repair order into PGCIL approval of the Company's HVDC manufacturing technology, opening a high-margin segment few domestic players can serve.
- Grow the export channel into the North American and European grid-replacement cycle, leveraging the 40-plus country footprint, the Fuji Electric technology licence and expanding high-voltage credentials; exports were approximately 4 percent of revenue as at end-December 2025, leaving substantial headroom.
- Pace fresh order intake selectively and deliberately, accepting only margin-accretive orders — the Company reported record revenue, its largest-ever order book and a conscious moderation of order intake in the same year.
- Tighten working capital through advance-collection requirements, stricter payment milestone structures in new contracts, intensified collections, and a formal policy of not accepting orders with delivery timelines beyond 24 months.
- Ramp the near-doubled Changodar and Moraiya capacity to convert operating leverage into margin, with results expected from FY28.
- Align the product range with renewable and green-hydrogen demand through solar-application transformers, green-hydrogen-application transformers and reactors for renewable evacuation, matching the Green Energy Corridor build-out.
- Retain scarce specialist engineering talent through the TARIL Employee Stock Option Plan 2024 and through technology-transfer programmes with Fuji Electric and ZTR, aligning employee and shareholder interests through the build phase.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: FY26 was the most intensive investment phase in TARIL's history, built around two pillars: capacity expansion at the Changodar and Moraiya plants, and the construction of four backward-integration facilities. Total installed capacity rose from 40,000 MVA in FY24 to approximately 75,000 MVA by the end of FY26, with additions of 22,000 MVA at Changodar and 15,000 MVA at Moraiya; against this installed base FY26 production reached a record 33,763 MVA, an utilisation rate of approximately 45 percent of the new total, which management describes as a deliberate build-ahead-of-demand strategy. On the backward-integration side, the Company commenced operations at four plants for CTC wire, bushings, pressboard and fabrication at a facility in Chiyada on the Sarkhej-Bavla Highway, secured a controlling stake in a CRGO processing facility, and obtained PGCIL approval for a fully automated radiator facility with tank manufacturing facility approval also initiated. Management has committed Rs 900-1000 crore of capital expenditure over the next fifteen months structured across three pillars — capacity expansion at Changodar and Moraiya (Rs ~150-200 crore), backward integration for CTC, pressboard, RIP bushings and fabrication (Rs 900-1000 crore), and testing and infrastructure including PGCIL-approvable facilities — funded through a combination of QIP proceeds, a leasing arrangement, internal accruals and existing credit lines. Commissioning is targeted between H2 FY27 for the initial facilities and Q1 FY28 for full operational capability, with full backward integration targeted by the first quarter of FY 2027-28. Execution has slipped in places: management disclosed that the Changodar capacity addition was delayed by four to five months and that full backward integration has slipped slightly owing to slow site progress and late arrival of plant and machinery, deferring the operating leverage on which the FY28 margin recovery depends. The expansion is also reflected in people and testing infrastructure — the workforce was expanded substantially to staff the ramp, and the NABL-accredited electrical-steel testing laboratory at Moraiya, the only such facility in the Indian transformer industry, together with PGCIL approvals secured for reactors at the Changodar testing facility, underpins the product-qualification capability the new capacity requires.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- A nationally mandated transmission super-cycle: the National Electricity Plan (Volume II, Transmission) commits over Rs 9.15 lakh crore to transmission investment through 2032, executed through PGCIL, state transmission utilities and private transmission licensees, with grid transformation capacity to rise from approximately 1,429 GVA in February 2026 to 2,345 GVA by 2032.
- A structural gap between Indian transformer manufacturing capacity (estimated around 450,000 MVA and already at high utilisation in higher-voltage categories) and the Plan's demand trajectory — the commercial foundation on which industry-wide expansion is being built, with the CEA estimating India needs to add 776,330 MVA of transformer capacity by FY27.
- Migration of demand up the voltage and complexity curve: as voltage class rises, the number of qualified manufacturers falls sharply, realisations per MVA climb, and EBITDA margins widen from approximately 10-13 percent for distribution transformers to 16-20 percent for large power transformers and 25 percent or more for specialised products.
- Renewable integration demand: India added over 30 GW of renewable capacity in FY26, and Green Energy Corridors connecting renewable-rich western states with eastern demand centres are major transformer and reactor consumers.
- Supply-side tightness: lead times have extended to 18-24 months for 400 kV and above transformers and 24-30 months for specialty products, benefiting established high-capacity manufacturers with proven type-testing credentials because customers cannot switch suppliers without restarting procurement and approval processes.
- Global grid-replacement export opportunity as North America and Europe face a simultaneous transformer replacement cycle on infrastructure installed in the 1970s and 1980s.
- Industrial electrification — electric arc furnaces replacing blast furnaces in steel, electric kilns in cement, electric boilers in process industries — generating a structural wave of demand for specialty transformers.
- Backward integration as a margin lever: gross margins currently stand in the range of 30-32 percent, and management expects them to expand toward 35 percent by FY28 and 40 percent at full integration as CTC, pressboard and RIP bushings facilities come online.
- Operating leverage from the capacity build: installed capacity has risen from 40,000 MVA to approximately 75,000 MVA against record FY26 production of 33,763 MVA, and as utilisation of the new capacity rises, fixed-cost absorption should support margins from FY28 when the Changodar and Moraiya expansions are expected to yield results.
- Management expects PAT growth to outpace revenue growth as operating leverage plays out and finance costs remain disciplined, and expects the working capital cycle to tighten progressively through FY27.
- A near-term counterweight: management characterises FY27 as a transition year in which working-capital discipline and execution — not demand — determine the quality of earnings; industry ordering saw a temporary pause in FY26 with fewer transmission schemes awarded, attributed to utility execution constraints rather than weakening demand.
- Unexecuted order book of Rs 5,005 crore as of 31 March 2026 (the Directors' Report states an order book position of Rs 5,008 crore as on the same date), described as the Company's largest-ever.
- Inquiries under active negotiation exceeding Rs 23,000 crore, providing revenue visibility well beyond the current year and allowing selective, margin-accretive order acceptance.
- Order book divided across segments: EPC players and state utilities are the two largest blocks, followed by central utilities, exports, industrial customers, the renewable segment, railways and third-party exports.
- Utilities accounted for approximately 44 percent of the unexecuted order book as at December 2025 and approximately 56 percent of in-year revenue.
- The Company secured its then-highest single order of Rs 740 crore from GETCO between 2024 and 2026.
- Management describes the order book as diversified and converting, and notes that improved order quality during FY26 is already translating into better payment term structures.

risks.note: Copper and CRGO dominate the cost base and copper-led inflation directly compressed FY26 margins. Management describes this as the Company's most material operational exposure because it cannot always be passed through on fixed-price contracts. Mitigation is order selection with better margins and payment terms, backward integration to internalise value, and price-variation clauses and hedging as natural further mitigants.
risks.risk: Raw-material price and availability risk — copper, electrical steel (CRGO) and transformer oil

risks.note: The Changodar expansion was delayed four to five months and full backward integration has slipped slightly owing to slow site progress and late arrival of plant and machinery. Delays defer the operating leverage on which the FY28 margin recovery depends, and execution risk is the key constraint the industry itself cites for the FY26 ordering slowdown. Mitigation is a staged commissioning plan with results expected from FY28 and backward-integration facilities fully operational from Q1 FY28.

The consolidated cash conversion cycle more than doubled to 199 days from 94 days, operating cash flow turned negative, and receivables rose roughly Rs 410 crore, meaning growth is currently funded through short-term borrowing. Until the cycle normalises this constrains the ability to fund growth internally. Mitigation is intensified collections, tightened order-acceptance terms with advance collection requirements, stricter payment milestones, and a conservative net-worth-to-borrowing position.
risks.risk: Stretched working-capital cycle and liquidity risk

risks.note: The Company operates in one product segment — transformer manufacturing, reported as a single segment under Ind AS 108 — with its principal manufacturing concentrated in the Ahmedabad region of Gujarat, exposing it to a single industry cycle and to location-specific operational disruption. Mitigation is the breadth of product applications across many end-markets and the multi-plant footprint within the cluster.

A further Rs 1000 crore of capex is planned over fifteen months, and funding this alongside a stretched working-capital cycle requires careful sequencing. Mitigation is a strengthened post-QIP equity base and modest gearing providing headroom.

High-voltage transformer manufacturing depends on scarce specialised design, winding and testing skills — insulation design engineering, high-voltage winding and tanking, impulse and short-circuit testing, thermal modelling and dielectric diagnostics — that cannot be acquired through standard technical education. Recruiting from this small national pool commands premium compensation, and the steep rise in employee benefit expense in FY26 reflects the cost of staffing the ramp.

India relies substantially on imported grain-oriented electrical steel, exposing manufacturers to currency and supply risk. Mitigation is the Company's NABL steel-testing capability and supplier relationships supporting quality assurance, though supply concentration remains.

Well-capitalised competitors are expanding aggressively — Hitachi Energy India alone reported an order backlog above Rs 29,500 crore as at March 2026, and players such as Voltamp, Atlanta Electricals and Shilchar are scaling — with competition sharpest in standard distribution and lower-voltage products. Separately, fewer utility transmission schemes were awarded in FY26 than in the prior year, and although attributed to execution rather than demand, a prolonged pause would pressure fresh order intake.

exports were approximately 4 percent of revenue as at end-December 2025, leaving substantial headroom.|Pace fresh order intake selectively and deliberately, accepting only margin-accretive orders — the Company reported record revenue, its largest-ever order book and a conscious moderation of order intake in the same year.|Tighten working capital through advance-collection requirements, stricter payment milestone structures in new contracts, intensified collections, and a formal policy of not accepting orders with delivery timelines beyond 24 months.|Ramp the near-doubled Changodar and Moraiya capacity to convert operating leverage into margin, with results expected from FY28.|Align the product range with renewable and green-hydrogen demand through solar-application transformers, green-hydrogen-application transformers and reactors for renewable evacuation, matching the Green Energy Corridor build-out.|Retain scarce specialist engineering talent through the TARIL Employee Stock Option Plan 2024 and through technology-transfer programmes with Fuji Electric and ZTR, aligning employee and shareholder interests through the build phase.
currentContext.expansion: FY26 was the most intensive investment phase in TARIL's history, built around two pillars: capacity expansion at the Changodar and Moraiya plants, and the construction of four backward-integration facilities. Total installed capacity rose from 40,000 MVA in FY24 to approximately 75,000 MVA by the end of FY26, with additions of 22,000 MVA at Changodar and 15,000 MVA at Moraiya; against this installed base FY26 production reached a record 33,763 MVA, an utilisation rate of approximately 45 percent of the new total, which management describes as a deliberate build-ahead-of-demand strategy. On the backward-integration side, the Company commenced operations at four plants for CTC wire, bushings, pressboard and fabrication at a facility in Chiyada on the Sarkhej-Bavla Highway, secured a controlling stake in a CRGO processing facility, and obtained PGCIL approval for a fully automated radiator facility with tank manufacturing facility approval also initiated. Management has committed Rs 900-1000 crore of capital expenditure over the next fifteen months structured across three pillars — capacity expansion at Changodar and Moraiya (Rs ~150-200 crore), backward integration for CTC, pressboard, RIP bushings and fabrication (Rs 900-1000 crore), and testing and infrastructure including PGCIL-approvable facilities — funded through a combination of QIP proceeds, a leasing arrangement, internal accruals and existing credit lines. Commissioning is targeted between H2 FY27 for the initial facilities and Q1 FY28 for full operational capability, with full backward integration targeted by the first quarter of FY 2027-28. Execution has slipped in places: management disclosed that the Changodar capacity addition was delayed by four to five months and that full backward integration has slipped slightly owing to slow site progress and late arrival of plant and machinery, deferring the operating leverage on which the FY28 margin recovery depends. The expansion is also reflected in people and testing infrastructure — the workforce was expanded substantially to staff the ramp, and the NABL-accredited electrical-steel testing laboratory at Moraiya, the only such facility in the Indian transformer industry, together with PGCIL approvals secured for reactors at the Changodar testing facility, underpins the product-qualification capability the new capacity requires.
currentContext.mdna: A nationally mandated transmission super-cycle: the National Electricity Plan (Volume II, Transmission) commits over Rs 9.15 lakh crore to transmission investment through 2032, executed through PGCIL, state transmission utilities and private transmission licensees, with grid transformation capacity to rise from approximately 1,429 GVA in February 2026 to 2,345 GVA by 2032.|A structural gap between Indian transformer manufacturing capacity (estimated around 450,000 MVA and already at high utilisation in higher-voltage categories) and the Plan's demand trajectory — the commercial foundation on which industry-wide expansion is being built, with the CEA estimating India needs to add 776,330 MVA of transformer capacity by FY27.|Migration of demand up the voltage and complexity curve: as voltage class rises, the number of qualified manufacturers falls sharply, realisations per MVA climb, and EBITDA margins widen from approximately 10-13 percent for distribution transformers to 16-20 percent for large power transformers and 25 percent or more for specialised products.|Renewable integration demand: India added over 30 GW of renewable capacity in FY26, and Green Energy Corridors connecting renewable-rich western states with eastern demand centres are major transformer and reactor consumers.|Supply-side tightness: lead times have extended to 18-24 months for 400 kV and above transformers and 24-30 months for specialty products, benefiting established high-capacity manufacturers with proven type-testing credentials because customers cannot switch suppliers without restarting procurement and approval processes.|Global grid-replacement export opportunity as North America and Europe face a simultaneous transformer replacement cycle on infrastructure installed in the 1970s and 1980s.|Industrial electrification — electric arc furnaces replacing blast furnaces in steel, electric kilns in cement, electric boilers in process industries — generating a structural wave of demand for specialty transformers.|Backward integration as a margin lever: gross margins currently stand in the range of 30-32 percent, and management expects them to expand toward 35 percent by FY28 and 40 percent at full integration as CTC, pressboard and RIP bushings facilities come online.|Operating leverage from the capacity build: installed capacity has risen from 40,000 MVA to approximately 75,000 MVA against record FY26 production of 33,763 MVA, and as utilisation of the new capacity rises, fixed-cost absorption should support margins from FY28 when the Changodar and Moraiya expansions are expected to yield results.|Management expects PAT growth to outpace revenue growth as operating leverage plays out and finance costs remain disciplined, and risks.risk: Raw-material price and availability risk — copper, electrical steel (CRGO) and transformer oil
risks.note: Copper and CRGO dominate the cost base and copper-led inflation directly compressed FY26 margins. Management describes this as the Company's most material operational exposure because it cannot always be passed through on fixed-price contracts. Mitigation is order selection with better margins and payment terms, backward integration to internalise value, and price-variation clauses and hedging as natural further mitigants.

The Changodar expansion was delayed four to five months and full backward integration has slipped slightly owing to slow site progress and late arrival of plant and machinery. Delays defer the operating leverage on which the FY28 margin recovery depends, and execution risk is the key constraint the industry itself cites for the FY26 ordering slowdown. Mitigation is a staged commissioning plan with results expected from FY28 and backward-integration facilities fully operational from Q1 FY28.

risks.risk: Stretched working-capital cycle and liquidity risk
risks.note: The consolidated cash conversion cycle more than doubled to 199 days from 94 days, operating cash flow turned negative, and receivables rose roughly Rs 410 crore, meaning growth is currently funded through short-term borrowing. Until the cycle normalises this constrains the ability to fund growth internally. Mitigation is intensified collections, tightened order-acceptance terms with advance collection requirements, stricter payment milestones, and a conservative net-worth-to-borrowing position.

The Company operates in one product segment — transformer manufacturing, reported as a single segment under Ind AS 108 — with its principal manufacturing concentrated in the Ahmedabad region of Gujarat, exposing it to a single industry cycle and to location-specific operational disruption. Mitigation is the breadth of product applications across many end-markets and the multi-plant footprint within the cluster.

A further Rs 1000 crore of capex is planned over fifteen months, and funding this alongside a stretched working-capital cycle requires careful sequencing. Mitigation is a strengthened post-QIP equity base and modest gearing providing headroom.

High-voltage transformer manufacturing depends on scarce specialised design, winding and testing skills — insulation design engineering, high-voltage winding and tanking, impulse and short-circuit testing, thermal modelling and dielectric diagnostics — that cannot be acquired through standard technical education. Recruiting from this small national pool commands premium compensation, and the steep rise in employee benefit expense in FY26 reflects the cost of staffing the ramp.

India relies substantially on imported grain-oriented electrical steel, exposing manufacturers to currency and supply risk. Mitigation is the Company's NABL steel-testing capability and supplier relationships supporting quality assurance, though supply concentration remains.

risks.risk: Intensifying competition and an industry-wide ordering pause
risks.note: Well-capitalised competitors are expanding aggressively — Hitachi Energy India alone reported an order backlog above Rs 29,500 crore as at March 2026, and players such as Voltamp, Atlanta Electricals and Shilchar are scaling — with competition sharpest in standard distribution and lower-voltage products. Separately, fewer utility transmission schemes were awarded in FY26 than in the prior year, and although attributed to execution rather than demand, a prolonged pause would pressure fresh order intake.

risks.risk: Receivables credit risk and product-approval dependency
risks.note: A large share of receivables sits with utilities and EPC customers whose payment cycles can be long, though the predominantly government-backed and blue-chip customer base lowers default risk. Sales to PGCIL and state utilities also depend on type-approvals, testing accreditation and utility procurement and tariff frameworks, mitigated by the NABL-accredited steel-testing laboratory and PGCIL approvals secured for reactors at the Changodar testing facility.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Transformers and Rectifiers (India) Limited manufactures power, furnace, rectifier, distribution and specialty transformers together with series and shunt reactors, and reports a single segment of transformer manufacturing under Ind AS 108. demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- A nationally mandated transmission super-cycle: the National Electricity Plan (Volume II, Transmission) commits over Rs 9.15 lakh crore to transmission investment through 2032, executed through PGCIL, state transmission utilities and private transmission licensees, with grid transformation capacity to rise from approximately 1,429 GVA in February 2026 to 2,345 GVA by 2032.
- A structural gap between Indian transformer manufacturing capacity (estimated around 450,000 MVA and already at high utilisation in higher-voltage categories) and the Plan's demand trajectory — the commercial foundation on which industry-wide expansion is being built, with the CEA estimating India needs to add 776,330 MVA of transformer capacity by FY27.
- Migration of demand up the voltage and complexity curve: as voltage class rises, the number of qualified manufacturers falls sharply, realisations per MVA climb, and EBITDA margins widen from approximately 10-13 percent for distribution transformers to 16-20 percent for large power transformers and 25 percent or more for specialised products.
- Renewable integration demand: India added over 30 GW of renewable capacity in FY26, and Green Energy Corridors connecting renewable-rich western states with eastern demand centres are major transformer and reactor consumers.
- Supply-side tightness: lead times have extended to 18-24 months for 400 kV and above transformers and 24-30 months for specialty products, benefiting established high-capacity manufacturers with proven type-testing credentials because customers cannot switch suppliers without restarting procurement and approval processes.
- Global grid-replacement export opportunity as North America and Europe face a simultaneous transformer replacement cycle on infrastructure installed in the 1970s and 1980s.
- Industrial electrification — electric arc furnaces replacing blast furnaces in steel, electric kilns in cement, electric boilers in process industries — generating a structural wave of demand for specialty transformers.
- Backward integration as a margin lever: gross margins currently stand in the range of 30-32 percent, and management expects them to expand toward 35 percent by FY28 and 40 percent at full integration as CTC, pressboard and RIP bushings facilities come online.
- Operating leverage from the capacity build: installed capacity has risen from 40,000 MVA to approximately 75,000 MVA against record FY26 production of 33,763 MVA, and as utilisation of the new capacity rises, fixed-cost absorption should support margins from FY28 when the Changodar and Moraiya expansions are expected to yield results.
- Management expects PAT growth to outpace revenue growth as operating leverage plays out and finance costs remain disciplined, and expects the working capital cycle to tighten progressively through FY27.
- A near-term counterweight: management characterises FY27 as a transition year in which working-capital discipline and execution — not demand — determine the quality of earnings; industry ordering saw a temporary pause in FY26 with fewer transmission schemes awarded, attributed to utility execution constraints rather than weakening demand.
- Unexecuted order book of Rs 5,005 crore as of 31 March 2026 (the Directors' Report states an order book position of Rs 5,008 crore as on the same date), described as the Company's largest-ever.
- Inquiries under active negotiation exceeding Rs 23,000 crore, providing revenue visibility well beyond the current year and allowing selective, margin-accretive order acceptance.
- Order book divided across segments: EPC players and state utilities are the two largest blocks, followed by central utilities, exports, industrial customers, the renewable segment, railways and third-party exports.
- Utilities accounted for approximately 44 percent of the unexecuted order book as at December 2025 and approximately 56 percent of in-year revenue.
- The Company secured its then-highest single order of Rs 740 crore from GETCO between 2024 and 2026.
- Management describes the order book as diversified and converting, and notes that improved order quality during FY26 is already translating into better payment term structures.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: FY26 was the most intensive investment phase in TARIL's history, built around two pillars: capacity expansion at the Changodar and Moraiya plants, and the construction of four backward-integration facilities. Total installed capacity rose from 40,000 MVA in FY24 to approximately 75,000 MVA by the end of FY26, with additions of 22,000 MVA at Changodar and 15,000 MVA at Moraiya; against this installed base FY26 production reached a record 33,763 MVA, an utilisation rate of approximately 45 percent of the new total, which management describes as a deliberate build-ahead-of-demand strategy. On the backward-integration side, the Company commenced operations at four plants for CTC wire, bushings, pressboard and fabrication at a facility in Chiyada on the Sarkhej-Bavla Highway, secured a controlling stake in a CRGO processing facility, and obtained PGCIL approval for a fully automated radiator facility with tank manufacturing facility approval also initiated. Management has committed Rs 900-1000 crore of capital expenditure over the next fifteen months structured across three pillars — capacity expansion at Changodar and Moraiya (Rs ~150-200 crore), backward integration for CTC, pressboard, RIP bushings and fabrication (Rs 900-1000 crore), and testing and infrastructure including PGCIL-approvable facilities — funded through a combination of QIP proceeds, a leasing arrangement, internal accruals and existing credit lines. Commissioning is targeted between H2 FY27 for the initial facilities and Q1 FY28 for full operational capability, with full backward integration targeted by the first quarter of FY 2027-28. Execution has slipped in places: management disclosed that the Changodar capacity addition was delayed by four to five months and that full backward integration has slipped slightly owing to slow site progress and late arrival of plant and machinery, deferring the operating leverage on which the FY28 margin recovery depends. The expansion is also reflected in people and testing infrastructure — the workforce was expanded substantially to staff the ramp, and the NABL-accredited electrical-steel testing laboratory at Moraiya, the only such facility in the Indian transformer industry, together with PGCIL approvals secured for reactors at the Changodar testing facility, underpins the product-qualification capability the new capacity requires.

MD Mamtora crisp on HVDC/exports; CFO Mehul Shah detailed on balance sheet. EY-IR appointment + fast reporting framed as governance upgrades.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Extra-high-voltage engineering credentials: the Company built and dispatched a 333 MVA, 1200 kV auto transformer to PowerGrid's National Test Station at Bina, described as the highest AC voltage transformer in the world, and competes across the 110 kV to 1200 kV range where the number of technically qualified manufacturers falls sharply.
- Sole NABL-accredited electrical-steel testing laboratory in the Indian transformer industry, providing independent and traceable test results that serve as both a quality control and a commercial credential.
- Technology licences from Fuji Electric of Japan for 400 kV and 765 kV class reactors and generator transformers, plus a strategic alliance with ZTR Ukraine for 765 kV transformer technology, embedding continuous access to advanced global engineering practice.
- First Indian company to receive an HVDC converter transformer repair order from PowerGrid, creating a pathway to PGCIL approval of HVDC manufacturing technology that very few competitors could claim.
- Furnace-transformer franchise with among the world's largest EAF transformer ratings, including a tested 220/253 MVA electric arc furnace transformer.
- Switching costs and qualification barriers: customers cannot simply switch suppliers without restarting procurement and approval processes, and lead times of 18-24 months for 400 kV and above transformers deepen the order-book advantage of established manufacturers with proven type-testing credentials.
- Blue-chip and diversified customer base spanning PGCIL, NTPC, GETCO, UPPTCL, RRVPNL, MPPTCL and WBSECL on the utility side, Siemens, Adani, Tata Power, ReNew Power, Torrent Power and AVAADA Energy in industry and renewables, and Jindal Steel & Power, JSW, SAIL and Hindustan Zinc in metals — repeat-order relationships built order after order rather than one-off wins.
- Backward integration into CTC, bushings, pressboard and fabrication capturing margin previously paid away to third-party suppliers, evidenced by a consolidated EBITDA margin running approximately 230 basis points above standalone.
- Export footprint across 40-plus countries with relationships including ABB, ArcelorMittal, Fluor, Siemens Energy, Danieli and the Novorossiysk Group, positioned for the North American and European grid-replacement cycle.

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body:
- **Changodar downtime** is the dominant risk — it single-handedly capped growth at +10% while peers did 50–60%; Q3FY27 recovery is a mgmt promise, not yet delivered.
- **CRGO DGTR anti-dumping duty** — potential RM-cost inflation; unresolved.
- **Working-capital/inventory build** — deliberate RM stocking to Dec-2026 raises interest cost near-term; unwind depends on backward-integration coming online on time.
- **Guidance-vs-reality gap** — 25% FY27 growth needs a very strong H2 after a soft H1; $1bn/FY29 implies ~50% CAGR, reframed to ~INR 8,000 cr (analysts openly pressed the math).
- **Execution stacking** — five backward-integration plants + two capacity expansions + HVDC all commissioning across FY27–28; slippage risk is high (Changodar already slipped once).
- **Management change** — new CFO Mehul Shah; IR outsourced to EY (governance-signalling after prior-year churn).

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body:
- **This is a timing air-pocket, not a demand miss** — order book +26%, inflow +218%, INR 23,000 cr pipeline; the growth simply sits behind an August-2026 Changodar restart. The Q3FY27 inflection is the whole thesis.
- **The $1bn target quietly shrank** from INR 9,600 cr to ~INR 8,000 cr (rupee reframing) — a soft downgrade dressed as an FX technicality; watch whether even INR 8,000 cr by FY29 holds given a soft FY27 base (~INR 2,500 cr FY26 → needs huge FY28–29).
- **Backward integration is now a revenue line, not just a margin lever** — INR 800–1,000 cr third-party sales feed the top-line target, so its commissioning cadence (CTC→Pressboard→Bushing→Fabrication) is doubly load-bearing.
- **Inventory build is a strategic hedge, not distress** — RM secured to Dec-2026; the interest drag is a deliberate insurance premium against geopolitical/CRGO supply shocks.
- Consol margin (19.2%) already runs well above the 16% standalone guide — subsidiaries are the quiet margin engine.

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- Move deliberately up the voltage and complexity curve — prioritising high-margin, niche and specialty products (EHV, 1200 kV, furnace, HVDC) — as a competitive response to intense, margin-dilutive competition at the 220 kV and below level.
- Deepen backward integration to internalise CTC, pressboard, RIP bushings and fabrication, replacing input-cost volatility with a captive, quality-controlled supply chain; each facility operationalised is expected to contribute 200-300 basis points of incremental EBITDA margin.
- Establish an HVDC entry pathway by converting the PGCIL converter-transformer …

themes.title: Transformer & grid-component shortage
themes.need: Transformer makers are running flat-out at record order books even as core-capacity ramps land (ATLANTAELE 16k->63k MVA, Q1FY27 record order book INR3,117cr on record INR972cr quarterly inflow, Vadod now PGCIL 400kV-approved with a 765kV tech tie-up in final talks; TARIL toward 75k+ MVA, Q1FY27 UEOB INR6,630cr +26% YoY on a >INR1,000cr single-shot PGCIL Ultra-Mega order, though a Changodar-expansion air-pocket held Q1 revenue to +10%; SHILCTECH adding 220kV) yet the binding constraint is still everything INSIDE a transformer - CRGO core steel, CTC/winding wire (KSHINTL/BHAGYANGR), bushings/insulators (YASHHV; 18-24mo lead, ~95% RIP/OIP imported) and transformer oil (APARINDS); both OEMs are now backward-integrating to own the bottleneck (TARIL's INR900-1,000cr CRGO/CTC/bushing/pressboard programme). Capacity-gated supply is the repeated 'need of the hour' and is driving pricing power now, though both OEMs flagged ~60,000 MVA of new 400kV capacity landing industry-wide in 3-4 months as a 1-year-out overcapacity watch-item (neither sees pricing pressure yet).
themes.driver: PGCIL Ultra-Mega order conversion (TARIL's first >INR1,000cr single-shot award) + Vadod/Changodar capacity ramps; 400kV short-circuit tests and 765kV PGCIL approvals due by Q2FY27-end are the next re-rating triggers; TARIL's Changodar restart (Aug-2026) is the swing quarter for its own growth reacceleration.
